newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Africa air traffic rumpus eases as strikers split.
newsitem.headline: Africa air traffic rumpus eases as strikers split.

text.p: Air travel improved across West Africa on Thursday as air traffic controllers in 15 states appeared divided on a strike that disrupted Christmas flights.

Union leaders at the regional Agency for the Safety of Aerial Navigation (ASECNA) said they were extending their initial 48-hour strike by another 72 hours because authorities had not addressed their pay demands.
But controllers in key airports affected by the strike returned to work, allowing flights to operate normally across most of the region, airport officials said.
By late afternoon the stoppage, launched at dawn on Wednesday, had been called off in Abidjan, Dakar, Mali and Cotonou, airport officials said.

Controllers in Dakar where ASECNA has its headquarters, said they had asked their union headquarters in Burkina Faso to lift the strike order "on the basis of promises made to us by the minister of tourism and the management of ASECNA".
But strike leaders at the ASECNA workers union headquarters in Ouagadougou later announced an extension of the stoppage.

"We have decided to extend the action by 72 hours until further notice," said union leader Alexandre Damiba. He said, however, that an unnamed head of state in the region had offered his good offices to try and resolve the dispute.
Damiba also said authorities had reversed their suspension order on him which prompted the union to announce earlier that the strike would go on for an indefinite preiod.

Despite the announcement flights were operating normally in Abidjan, the hub of air travel in the region, airport officials said. Both Air France and Air Afrique, the dominant carriers at at the terminal, expected their intercontinental schedules to opertate fairly normally.
"All our scheduled flights are operating normally today," an airport duty official told Reuters.
Just about all ASECNA members are former French colonies in West and Central Africa and the Indian Ocean.

The strike also affected non-Francophone neighouring states, but among the worst hit carriers was Air France which has several flights to the region. More than half a dozen such flights from Paris were cancelled on Christmas Day.

In Paris, some 238 French tourists whose Christmas holidays in Africa were cancelled due to the strike briefly took a travel agent and a hotel manager "hostage" in protest against their plight, French media said on Thursday.
The tourists were aboard a chartered aircraft which had to head back to France on Tuesday when it reached the halfway point of a Paris to Dakar, Senegal, radios and newspapers said.
The frustrated travellers, who had paid for a luxury Christmas Eve dinner on an exotic West African beach, found themselves ushered instead into a dreary airport hotel outside Paris late at night.
The "hostages" were finally released when police arrived and advised the travellers to file charges against the travel agency.
